procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a Sessions Court or similar trial court in Bombay, as the High Court confirmation case suggests a death sentence was initially imposed.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated December 18, 1962 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 1426 of 1968 and confirmation Case No. 21 of 1968.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Bombay High Court dismissed the appeal of Moti alias Narayan Shesharina Yadav (accused No. 2) and Sheshanna Bhumanna Yadav (accused No. 3). However, the High Court altered the conviction of accused No. 2 from Section 302 (murder) to Section 302 read with Section 120B (criminal conspiracy) and Section 302 read with Section 34 (common intention) of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court confirmed the death sentence for accused No. 3, but reduced the punishment of accused No. 2 (who was 17 years old at the time) to rigorous imprisonment for life.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court appeal was initiated by special leave. The appeal challenges the Bombay High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the appeal.

directions: The accused will surrender to his bail, if any.

issue.issue_text: whether there was corroboration in regard to the crime.

facts: Two accused, a father and son, were convicted of murdering a young boy and committing theft from the house where the boy was living.
The main evidence against them was the testimony of an approver named Dinkar.

Corroborating evidence against the son (accused No. 2) included: being seen with the victim on the day of the crime, producing stolen cloth, selling stolen items (cycle carrier, utensils), and hastily retrieving a stolen cloth from a tailor.

Corroborating evidence against the father (accused No. 3) included: having a motive (disputes with the victim's grandfather), selling stolen articles, and joining his son in the sale of a stolen cycle carrier.
The murder and the theft occurred in close proximity, suggesting they were part of the same event.
law: The law regarding an approver's evidence requires caution; while an accomplice is a competent witness, it is generally unsafe to convict on their testimony alone without corroboration (based on sections 133 and 114 of the Evidence Act).

A three-part test must be satisfied: (1) the approver must be a reliable witness, (2) there must be reliable corroboration of the approver's evidence, and (3) the corroboration must be sufficient in material particulars to connect the accused with the crime.
Corroboration is confirmatory evidence that can come from another witness or from circumstances, such as the conduct of the accused.
The corroborative evidence must confirm the part of the testimony that suggests the crime was committed by the accused, not just any part of the story.
application: The Court first determined that the approver, Dinkar, was a reliable witness, satisfying the first part of the legal test.
The Court then identified numerous pieces of evidence that corroborated the approver's testimony and connected both the father and son to the criminal events.
The Court reasoned that the murder and the theft were not separate incidents but formed a single, "composite unit" or transaction due to their close proximity in time.

Because the events were part of the same transaction, the evidence that corroborated the accuseds' involvement in the theft (such as their joint disposal of stolen articles) also served as sufficient corroboration for their involvement in the murder.
The close association of the father and son in disposing of the stolen goods further strengthened the corroboration against both of them for the entire transaction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that there was sufficient corroboration. It held that the murder and theft were part of a single transaction, and therefore, the evidence corroborating the accuseds' involvement in the theft also served to corroborate the approver's testimony regarding their participation in the murder, proving they were guilty of the offenses with which they were charged.

issue.issue_text: whether there was corroboration in regard to accused No. 2 and 3 being guilty of the offence.

facts.fact: For Accused No. 2 (the son), corroborating evidence included: his statement leading to the discovery of stolen articles; being seen with the victim by two different witnesses on the day of the murder; producing a piece of cloth identical to the victim's mattress cover; and selling or pledging multiple stolen items (a cycle, utensils, a cycle carrier) that were identified by the victim's family.

For Accused No. 3 (the father), corroborating evidence included: a motive, as he was in civil and criminal disputes with the victim's grandfather; his name being in a witness's notebook; giving stolen silver and utensils to a witness (Takalkar) for sale and storage; and joining his son (Accused No. 2) in selling the stolen cycle carrier.
The court noted the close relationship (father and son) and their joint actions in disposing of the stolen property.

law.law_text: Corroboration is confirmatory evidence that can come from another witness or from circumstances, such as the conduct of the accused.
Corroborative evidence must confirm the part of the testimony that suggests the crime was committed by the accused.

application.application_text: The Court determined that the murder and the theft were not separate events but a single, 'composite unit' or transaction, linked by the close proximity of time.

Because the theft and murder were considered one transaction, the substantial evidence corroborating the accuseds' involvement in the theft (possessing and selling stolen items) also served as sufficient corroboration for their involvement in the murder.

The Court found that the numerous pieces of evidence, such as the disposal of stolen goods by both accused and the motive of Accused No. 3, directly implicated them in the crime, thus confirming the material particulars of the approver's testimony as required by law.
The close association of the father and son in disposing of the stolen articles pointed to the 'inescapable conclusion' that they acted together as part of the same transaction.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that there was sufficient corroboration for the guilt of both Accused No. 2 and 3. It affirmed the High Court's conclusion that the evidence proved they were guilty of the offences, finding no infirmity in the evidence against them.

issue.issue_text: whether there was corroboration in regard to the approver's story about the conspiracy and the common intention by way of a pre-conceived plan to murder Narendra.

facts.fact: The murder and the subsequent theft of items from the victim's house were considered to be a single, 'composite unit' or transaction.
Accused No. 3 had a motive to commit the crime, stemming from civil and criminal disputes with the victim's grandfather, Dr. Nanavati, over a bungalow.
Accused No. 3 proposed the murder to the approver, Dinkar, and suggested that his own son, Accused No. 2, should also be involved.
Accused No. 3 was directly linked to the disposal of the stolen property. He gave silver articles to a witness, Takalkar, to sell, and these items were later recovered by the police and identified.
Witnesses saw the victim, Narendra, alive in the company of Accused No. 2 and the approver shortly before the murder.
The approver led police to the place where the victim's remains (skull, bone, hair) and belongings (a shirt and chain, identified by family) were discovered.

law.law: To rely on an approver's testimony, the court must first be satisfied that the approver is a reliable witness.
Once reliability is established, the approver's evidence requires corroboration in material particulars that connect the accused with the crime.

application.application: The Court first determined that the approver, Dinkar, was a reliable witness.

The Court then linked the murder and the theft as parts of the same transaction. It reasoned that since the events were a 'composite unit,' evidence corroborating the accused's involvement in the theft also served to corroborate their involvement in the entire conspiracy, including the murder.

The evidence of Accused No. 3 disposing of the stolen goods, the close association between the accused, and the proximity in time between the murder and theft were all seen as material particulars that corroborated the approver's story of a pre-conceived plan.
The testimony of independent witnesses placing the victim with the accused, and the discovery of the victim's remains based on the approver's information, further strengthened the approver's account.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the High Court's conclusion that there was sufficient corroboration of the approver's evidence. The key to this decision was treating the murder and theft as a single transaction, which allowed evidence related to the theft to corroborate the approver's testimony about the entire conspiracy and the common intention to murder.

arguments.issue_text: whether there was corroboration in regard to the crime.
appellant_arguments: There was no corroboration of the actual participation in the murder.
Accused No. 3 could be guilty of theft but not of murder.
respondent_arguments: There was sufficient corroboration of the evidence which connected accused No. 2 and 3 not only with the offence of theft but also with murder.

Corroborating evidence included: civil and criminal proceedings between accused No. 3 and the deceased's grandfather (motive); accused No. 3 selling articles belonging to the deceased's grandfather; and the washerman's testimony placing accused No. 2 and the approver with a boy matching the deceased's description.

arguments.issue_text: whether there was corroboration in regard to accused No. 2 and 3 being guilty of the offence.
appellant_arguments: There was no corroboration of the actual participation of accused No. 2 and 3 in the murder.
respondent_arguments: There was sufficient corroboration of the approver's evidence in material particulars to prove accused No. 2 and 3 were guilty.

Evidence against accused No. 3 included: pre-existing civil and criminal proceedings with the deceased's family; selling articles identified as belonging to the deceased's grandfather; giving a piece of cloth to the approver; and joining his son (accused No. 2) in the sale of a cycle carrier.
Evidence against accused No. 2 included: the discovery of articles in a godown as a result of his statement and the washerman's testimony placing him with the deceased.

arguments.issue_text: whether there was corroboration in regard to the approver's story about the conspiracy and the common intention by way of a pre-conceived plan to murder Narendra.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's general argument that there was no corroboration for the murder implies there was no corroboration for a conspiracy or common intention to murder.
respondent_arguments: There was corroboration of the approver's evidence regarding the conspiracy and common intention.

The collective evidence, including the motive from prior disputes, the joint actions of the accused (like selling the cycle carrier), and the disposal of stolen goods, supported the existence of a pre-conceived plan.

cases.case_name: Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: For the law on corroboration of accomplice evidence, stating that the court must be satisfied that: (1) the approver is a reliable witness; (2) there is reliable corroboration of the approver's evidence; and (3) there is sufficient corroborative evidence in material particulars to connect the accused with the crime.

cases.case_name: Lachi Ram v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: For the law on corroboration of accomplice evidence, stating that the court must be satisfied that: (1) the approver is a reliable witness; (2) there is reliable corroboration of the approver's evidence; and (3) there is sufficient corroborative evidence in material particulars to connect the accused with the crime.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where multiple offenses form part of the same composite transaction due to close proximity in time and association, and an approver is found to be a reliable witness, evidence that provides sufficient corroboration of the approver's testimony in material particulars regarding the transaction is sufficient to prove guilt for all offenses within that transaction.
obiter: If a witness states that an accused stole sheep and placed the skins in a certain location, the discovery of the skins in that location does not corroborate the evidence against the accused. However, if the skins are found in the accused's house, it would serve as corroboration as it tends to confirm the accused's involvement in the theft.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the murder and the theft were not separate events but formed a single, composite transaction. Because the transaction was a unified whole and the approver was found to be a reliable witness, all the pieces of evidence corroborating the theft also served as sufficient corroboration for the murder, proving the accused were guilty of all offences with which they were charged.
legal_tests_applied: The law of corroboration of accomplice evidence as laid down in Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab, which requires that before the court would look into the corroborative evidence, it must be satisfied that the evidence of the approver is reliable.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's attempt to separate the crime of theft from the crime of murder failed, as the court found that the 'close proximity of time between the murder and theft points to the inescapable conclusion that they formed part of the same transaction.'
The court found the approver, Dinkar, to be a reliable witness, which is the first step required before considering corroborative evidence.
The court determined that the collective evidence sufficiently corroborated the approver's testimony in material particulars, connecting the accused to the composite crime of theft and murder.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully established that the murder and theft were a 'composite unit,' allowing evidence of one to corroborate the other.

The respondent provided sufficient corroborating evidence, which included: the motive of accused No. 3 arising from prior civil and criminal proceedings with the deceased's grandfather; the disposal of stolen articles by accused No. 3 to a witness named Takalkar; the discovery of other stolen articles as a result of a statement by accused No. 2; and the joint action of accused No. 2 and 3 in selling a stolen cycle carrier.
The court accepted the respondent's position that there was 'close association in the disposal of the articles' between the two accused, which supported the finding of a joint criminal enterprise.
policy_considerations: Due to the imposition of a capital sentence on accused No. 3, the court undertook a heightened level of scrutiny, stating: 'In view of the fact that there was capital sentence of accused No. 3 we went through the evidence to find out as to whether there was any infirmity in evidence. We have found none.'
